headline: Alibaba hikes DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 output prices by 230% overnight
summary: Alibaba dramatically increased DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 output costs by 230%, signaling an end to heavily subsidized AI compute. This trend forces builders to re-evaluate unit economics and optimize token usage.
details: Alibaba has raised the output price on DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 from $0.40 to $1.32 per million tokens, a 230% spike. Input costs for the model more than doubled, moving from $0.20 to $0.44 per million tokens.

These hikes are not isolated; Mistral increased its latest Ministral 3B and 8B models by 150% and 50% respectively. Alibaba's Qwen3.6 35B-A3B also saw a 52% output increase, with 17 distinct price movements observed across the board.
The sudden cost increases indicate that the era of heavily subsidized AI compute is ending. Labs are now passing the real costs of inference down to developers and businesses relying on their APIs.

For builders, this means the 'honeymoon is over,' requiring immediate optimization of prompts, aggressive caching of outputs, and a shift away from treating compute as an unlimited resource. Applications with agentic loops burning tokens without measurable revenue will see margins vanish.

The price adjustments expose the fragility of businesses built on the assumption of perpetually cheap tokens, leaving them vulnerable to market shifts. Only Zhipu AI moved aggressively in the opposite direction, slashing GLM-5V-Turbo prices by 85%.

Despite rising API costs, the underlying demand for programmable compute remains aggressive, evidenced by SF Compute's recent $245 million compute sale. This highlights intense competition for guaranteed compute capacity, making raw processing power expensive.

Meanwhile, Meta continues to push on both ends of the spectrum, debuting Muse Wonder Full (Max) as a top-tier model while also publishing Muse Glimmer, a 30B open-weight agentic model for single consumer GPU deployment. This strategy aims to compete on benchmarks and enable local development.

headline: 93% of candidates accept AI-written code in AI-assisted coding interviews
summary: A study of 438 practice AI-assisted coding interviews reveals that 93% of candidates accept AI-generated code. This trend is seen across practice rounds for companies like Amazon, Google, and Meta.
details: A study of 438 practice AI-assisted coding interviews found that candidates accepted AI-generated code 93% of the time. This trend was observed across practice rounds for ten major companies, including Shopify, Meta, Amazon, and Google.

When an AI assistant proposed code before the first submission, 87% of first submits passed the full test suite. This is a significant increase compared to the 53% pass rate when no AI proposal was given.

After passing tests, candidates were asked to explain the code. Only 9% provided complete explanations, while 79% were partial, often missing key points. A notable 29% skipped open-ended explanation questions.

The data suggests that in typical sessions, the AI writes the code, and the candidate primarily accepts it, focusing on getting tests to pass. The critical steps of checking the code and explaining its details are often overlooked in practice.

These findings are from practice sessions on nyrion.ai, not real interviews, and the assistant follows its own rules. The numbers reflect how people practice, not necessarily every company's specific interview round.
